consensus_summary: Ship primarily symbolizes the Church (Barque of Peter / ark typology) as the vessel of salvation carrying believers safely through the storms and dangers of the world/sea.
book_summary: Ship symbolizes an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding on the sea of peoples, crewed by inhabitants, guided by rulers, defended by armies, and carrying wealth as cargo; it may break while its people survive.
consensus_core_identification: the Church as vessel of salvation
boundary_disagreement: Book excludes the Church (and personal-faith voyage) as the proper core referent and reassigns the symbol to secular political entities; consensus treats political/commercial uses (Tyre, Tarshish, Babylon) only as secondary alternatives.
material_contradiction: The two cores cannot both be true of the same primary referent: identifying the ship with the Church requires rejecting the book's earthly-political identification, and vice versa.
rationale: Consensus (all four responses) settles on Church as primary via ark, gospel-boat, and patristic evidence, listing political/commercial ships only as alternatives. The book explicitly notes the common Church view yet replaces it with a political-body core drawn from the same commercial-judgment texts, producing contradictory central referents rather than a mere boundary shift or refinement of the Church category.
strongest_objection: The long-standing, near-universal patristic-to-modern identification of ship with Church (nave, Barque of Peter, ark typology) is simply set aside without engaging those primary gospel and Petrine texts.
